strengths: Addresses a challenging and practical task: scene-consistent camera-controllable video generation from arbitrary-length input video.
Proposes dual spatio-temporal conditioning that combines temporal frames for motion continuity with a static-only 3D scene memory for spatial consistency.
Introduces a dynamic masking pipeline using optical flow, CoTracker3, and SAM2 to separate static geometry from dynamic elements, enabling construction of a static point cloud for future generation.
Builds on a strong pretrained video generator (CogVideoX-I2V-5B) with minimal architectural changes, preserving learned video priors.
Evaluates on RealEstate10K and DynPose-100K with multiple metrics, showing improvements in scene consistency, camera controllability, and video quality over several baselines.
Qualitative results demonstrate better scene consistency and more faithful camera trajectory following than DFoT and other camera-control methods.
weaknesses: The central claim that spatial conditioning is necessary for scene consistency is not fully supported: there is no ablation of the full model without spatial conditioning (e.g., temporal-only or n=0). The ablation on n shows negligible differences between n=1 and n=7, undermining the benefit of multi-frame spatial retrieval.

Baseline comparisons are not fully fair or complete: camera-controllable baselines condition on a single image while the proposed method uses 9+ temporal frames plus 3D memory, without adapting baselines to receive comparable temporal context. DFoT comparison is unclear because DFoT may not accept camera trajectories, and no comparison is made to other video-to-future-video or geometry-grounded methods (e.g., Cosmos, Gen3C, TrajectoryCrafter).

The dynamic masking pipeline may be fragile for objects that enter or disappear during the video. The backward tracking and SAM2 prompting procedure is not fully specified, and it is unclear how points tracked back to t=0 correctly segment objects absent at the beginning.

Important technical details are missing, including the number of generated frames T, resolution, fps, optical-flow threshold tau, training data size, inference runtime/memory, and code availability. Efficiency claims are not empirically supported.

Long-horizon capability is not demonstrated: the method generates a single future chunk rather than evaluating autoregressive multi-chunk generation or very long outputs. The 'arbitrary-length' claim is therefore overstated for output generation.

The scene consistency evaluation protocol lacks detail: it is unclear how revisited viewpoints are selected and matched between generated and input frames, and how dynamic regions are masked for metrics. There is no analysis of the accuracy of the SLAM-estimated camera poses or the static point cloud.
Table 2 contains an incorrect arrow for mRotErr (shown as ↑ although lower error is better), which is a minor but confusing error.

Novelty is incremental: the method combines existing components (MegaSAM, SAM2, CoTracker3, CogVideoX) with a dual conditioning scheme, and similar static 3D memory conditioning has been explored in Gen3C for novel view synthesis.
There is no broader impact or ethical discussion, which is often expected for generative video models.

strengths: Addresses a challenging and practically relevant task: scene-consistent, camera-controllable future video generation from arbitrary-length input videos.
Proposes a conceptually reasonable dual spatio-temporal conditioning scheme that combines temporal continuity from recent frames with spatial consistency from a static 3D scene memory.
Introduces a dynamic masking pipeline using optical flow, CoTracker3, and SAM2 to extract static geometry, with an ablation showing its importance.
Builds on a strong pretrained video diffusion model (CogVideoX-I2V-5B) and leverages off-the-shelf SLAM/segmentation tools, which could be practical if properly validated.
Evaluates on two datasets (RealEstate10K and DynPose-100K) and reports multiple metrics for scene consistency, camera control, and video quality.
weaknesses: Evaluation is not a fair apples-to-apples comparison: baselines are image-to-video or text-to-video models with much less context, while the proposed method uses last 9 frames plus a 3D scene memory. No video-to-future-video baselines (e.g., Cosmos, Gen3C, ReCamMaster, TrajectoryCrafter) are compared under the same setting.
The closest baseline, DFoT, may not be camera-controllable; using it for camera-control and scene-consistency comparisons is questionable and likely biases results in the proposed method's favor.

The spatial conditioning provides warped static views at the target camera poses, so scene consistency and camera control may be largely achieved by copying from the condition. There is no ablation removing spatial conditioning (e.g., temporal-only) to isolate the actual generative contribution.

Training data leakage / unclear splits: RealEstate10K is used for training and also for evaluation; the paper does not specify that a held-out test split was used, making the RealEstate10K results unreliable.

Architecture description is unclear: it is not explained how temporal (w=9) and spatial (T) conditions are concatenated channel-wise while keeping the DiT backbone unchanged, given different numbers of frames and latent dimensions.

Ablation studies are insufficient: only n and dynamic masking are ablated. There is no ablation on the temporal window size, dual conditioning vs. alternatives, SLAM/pose accuracy, training data mixture, or inference with/without camera trajectory.

Dynamic masking pipeline has unaddressed failure cases: objects that appear after the first frame or are not present at t=0 may not be segmented, and thresholds/parameters for optical flow, CoTracker3, and SAM2 are not reported.

Computational efficiency claims are unsupported: no runtime or memory analysis is provided for arbitrary-length inputs, despite using dynamic SLAM, optical flow, point tracking, and SAM2 over the entire input video.

Evaluation protocol details are missing: how viewpoint matching is performed, how dynamic masks are obtained for generated videos, how many frames T are generated, and what resolution/duration are used.

Metric/table inconsistencies: mRotErr is marked with an up-arrow despite being an error metric; some improvements are very small (e.g., mRotErr 2.3977 vs 2.3772) and no statistical significance or variance is reported.
Qualitative results are limited to a few cherry-picked examples, with no user study or systematic analysis of failure cases.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release, incomplete training details (dataset size, filtering, captions, resolution, T, thresholds), and no limitations or broader-impact discussion.

strengths: Addresses a novel and challenging task: scene-consistent camera-controllable video generation from arbitrary-length video, with clear applications in film, VR, and synthetic data.

The dual spatio-temporal conditioning design elegantly separates temporal motion continuity (last few frames) from spatial scene consistency (projected static point clouds), allowing reuse of a strong pretrained video diffusion model with minimal architectural changes.

The 3D scene memory construction with dynamic masking (optical flow differences, CoTracker3 backward tracking, SAM2 propagation) is a well-motivated pipeline for extracting static geometry while avoiding ghosting and outdated dynamics; the ablation shows a clear benefit from dynamic masking.

Empirical results are generally strong: the method outperforms DFoT on scene/geometric consistency metrics and outperforms camera-controllable baselines on camera control and video quality across RealEstate10K and DynPose-100K.

The conditioning is computationally efficient in principle: using top-n spatially adjacent frames and channel-wise concatenation avoids quadratic scaling with input length, and no extra camera-control adapter is needed.
The paper is well-written with helpful figures and qualitative comparisons that illustrate the advantages of the proposed approach.
weaknesses: The scene-consistency comparison relies almost entirely on DFoT, and it is unclear how DFoT was adapted to follow camera trajectories, since DFoT is not originally a camera-controllable method. This makes the comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 difficult to interpret and potentially unfair.

The ablation on the number of spatially adjacent frames n is weak: performance differences are negligible (e.g., PSNR 13.0207 for n=1 vs. 13.0468 for n=7), and n=L sometimes achieves better MEt3R, so the choice n=7 is not strongly justified.

Important implementation details are missing or vague: the number of generated frames T, inference/preprocessing time, how user-specified camera trajectories are aligned with SLAM-estimated input poses, and how SLAM/masking failures are handled.

No ablation is provided for the temporal window size w, and there is no comparison against simple point-cloud warping or naive long-context conditioning to isolate the contribution of the diffusion model versus the spatial prompts.
The method depends on off-the-shelf dynamic SLAM, SAM2, and CoTracker3; robustness to errors or failures in these components is not evaluated, which limits confidence in real-world deployment.

There are minor inconsistencies and typos (e.g., mRotErr marked with ↑ although lower is better, MEt3R vs. Met3R, VBenchmark++ vs. VBenchmark+), and the paper lacks a broader impact/limitations discussion.

strengths: Addresses a new and challenging task: scene-consistent camera-controllable video generation from arbitrary-length input video, with clear practical applications.
Introduces a sensible dual spatio-temporal conditioning strategy that combines temporal frames for motion continuity and static-only 3D point cloud projections for spatial consistency.
The dynamic masking pipeline (optical flow, SAM2, CoTracker) for extracting static geometry and avoiding ghosting artifacts is well-motivated and thoroughly ablated.

Extensive experiments across RealEstate10K, DynPose-100K, and DAVIS, with metrics for scene consistency, camera controllability, and video quality; the 77% MEt3R error reduction over DFoT is particularly strong evidence for improved multi-view consistency.
Ablation studies validate the importance of dynamic masking and spatial prompts, and show that replacing MegaSAM with DepthAnything v3 improves results, demonstrating modularity.
Architectural changes are minimal and preserve pretrained CogVideoX priors; conditioning via channel concatenation is computationally efficient at generation time.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely an integration of existing components (dynamic SLAM, SAM2, CoTracker, point cloud projection, video diffusion), with the main contribution being the combination rather than a fundamentally new method.
Camera controllability improvements over DFoT are modest (e.g., mRotErr 2.3772 vs 2.3977; mCamMC 8.6352 vs 9.2330), so the claim of significantly better camera control is not strongly supported.

Camera controllability evaluation uses MegaSAM to estimate camera parameters from generated videos, while MegaSAM is also used to construct the 3D memory, potentially introducing bias; independent validation would strengthen the results.

Baseline comparisons for camera controllability include single-image conditioned methods (CameraCtrl, MotionCtrl, FloVD, AC3D) that receive less input information, making the comparison somewhat unfair; DFoT is closer, but gains are small.
The choice of n=7 spatial frames is not well justified: Table 4 shows n=1 already achieves PSNR 13.0207 vs n=7 13.0468, indicating marginal benefit from additional spatial frames.

The arbitrary-length video claim is not fully demonstrated; SLAM over long sequences may be expensive and memory-heavy, and long-video generation is only evaluated in the appendix with autoregressive error accumulation.

Missing comparisons to recent concurrent works on 3D memory/world models (e.g., SPMem, WorldMem, Gen3C) and newer camera-controllable methods (e.g., CameraCtrl II, Seaweed-APT2), limiting positioning.
Some claims are overstated, e.g., 'precise camera control without any other explicit camera conditioning,' when the target camera trajectory is still explicitly used to render the spatial prompts.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging task: scene-consistent camera-controllable video generation from arbitrary-length video, with applications in film, VR, and synthetic data.
Proposes a sensible dual spatio-temporal conditioning idea: temporal frames for motion continuity and projected static point clouds for scene consistency.
Introduces a three-stage dynamic masking pipeline combining optical flow, SAM2, and CoTracker3 to extract static geometry from dynamic videos.
Modular design leverages off-the-shelf dynamic SLAM and CogVideoX, allowing components to be swapped (e.g., DepthAnything v3) without retraining the full backbone.
Extensive experiments on RealEstate10K, DynPose-100K, and DAVIS with multiple metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, MEt3R, camera controllability, FVD, VBench).
Ablations on dynamic masking, number of spatial frames, temporal window size, and masking stages provide some insight into component contributions.
Qualitative comparisons and visualizations demonstrate improved scene consistency and camera control over several baselines.
Clear motivation, well-organized presentation, and a reproducibility statement indicating code will be released.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core is an integration of existing tools (dynamic SLAM, SAM2, CoTracker3, point cloud projection, CogVideoX). The dynamic masking pipeline is a combination of off-the-shelf methods rather than a new model or learning objective.

Unclear conditioning mechanism: how Temporal(w) and Spatial(T) are concatenated channel-wise when they have different temporal lengths (w=9 vs T generated frames) is not explained. The claim that the DiT backbone remains entirely unchanged is inconsistent with adding conditioning channels; the zero-padding slots explanation in the appendix is insufficient.

Inconsistent experimental numbers between the main paper and appendix. For example, dynamic masking ablations in Table 4 and Table 6 disagree, and Table 6 shows better MEt3R without dynamic masking, contradicting the main claim.

Weak ablation for number of spatial frames: n=1 performs nearly as well as n=7 on PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, with only n=0 clearly worse. This undermines the necessity of aggregating multiple spatially adjacent frames.

Missing evaluation on novel or unobserved viewpoints. The task explicitly includes exploring nearby regions and extrapolating unseen content, but all scene-consistency evaluations only revisit seen viewpoints. The method likely fails when target views do not overlap input views because spatial prompts become empty; no failure cases or quantitative analysis are provided.

Missing strong baselines: no comparison to Gen3C, SPMem, WorldMem, CameraCtrl2, or Seaweed-APT2 despite discussing them as related. Only DFoT is used for scene consistency, and it is unclear how DFoT was adapted for camera control, making the comparison potentially unfair.
Camera controllability improvements are modest (e.g., mRotErr 2.3977 vs 2.3772; mCamMC 9.2330 vs 8.6352), yet the paper claims significant and precise camera control.
Long-video evaluation on DAVIS is unclear: DAVIS lacks camera trajectories, so how RMSE/MSE/ATE are computed is not explained, and the comparison excludes DFoT and other relevant long-video methods.

Overstated claims: arbitrary-length input and negligible computational overhead are not supported. SLAM processing scales with input length, and inference with MegaSAM is slower than FloVD (9 min vs 8 min). Training data also filters out excessive camera motion, limiting generalizability.

Dynamic masking limitations are not addressed: objects entering later frames, backward tracking failures, and threshold sensitivity are not analyzed, and no mask quality metrics (e.g., IoU) are reported.

Reproducibility details are missing: threshold tau, point sampling counts, z-buffering/occlusion handling in point cloud projection, spatial adjacency computation, and exact training data filtering are not specified.
Ethical considerations are not discussed, despite the potential for misuse of controllable video generation for deepfakes or misinformation.

strengths: Proposes a new task and practical framework for scene-consistent camera-controllable video generation from arbitrary-length input videos.
Introduces dual spatio-temporal conditioning that jointly leverages temporal frames for motion continuity and spatial projections from a static 3D scene memory for long-range scene consistency.
Develops a dynamic masking pipeline using optical flow, SAM2, and CoTracker3 to extract static geometry from dynamic videos, with ablation studies showing its importance.
Achieves strong quantitative improvements in scene consistency (e.g., 77% MEt3R error reduction) and video quality (FVD, VBench) on DynPose-100K and RealEstate10K.
Provides extensive ablations on temporal window size, number of spatial frames, and dynamic masking stages, supporting design choices.
Shows modularity by swapping SLAM backends (MegaSAM vs. DepthAnything v3) and reports inference time, indicating practical efficiency.
weaknesses: The architecture for integrating dual spatio-temporal conditions is unclear: the paper claims channel-wise concatenation of latents while also claiming the DiT backbone remains unchanged, which is contradictory unless further details are provided.

Scene-consistency evaluation only compares against DFoT; other camera-controllable baselines are not evaluated on scene consistency, and the camera controllability improvement over DFoT is marginal (e.g., mRotErr 2.377 vs 2.397).
Baselines are not given the same input context: our method uses arbitrary-length video, while I2V/T2V baselines use a single image or text, making comparisons inherently unequal.
The dynamic masking pipeline may fail for objects that appear later or are never visible in the first frame; extreme viewpoint extrapolation and very long inputs are not thoroughly evaluated.
No ethical or broader-impact discussion is provided, which is important for video generation techniques with potential misuse (e.g., deepfakes).

The evaluation protocol for scene consistency relies on estimated camera poses from generated videos (using MegaSAM), which could introduce bias since MegaSAM is also used in the method's 3D memory construction.
